extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, poets, and letter-writers; literary correspondents
extracted.subtask_description: Practical stylistic and professional guidance for writers and poets, covering poetic diction, realistic narrative technique, epistolary presentation, and career advice about authorship and booksellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poetry slang / provincial phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry _slang_ of every kind is to be avoided. There is a rustic Cockneyism, as little pleasing as ours of London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overload poems with local provincialisms unless they contribute materially to expression. Occasional home-rustic terms may be 'fresh and startling,' but when 'nothing is gained in expression, it is out of tenor.' Mixing 'barbarous with refined phrases' prevents broader appreciation; study Shenstone for a model of the true rustic style. (Anti-pattern: transplanting Arcadia to Helpstone or gratuitous provincialism that startles without adding value.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter-of-fact narrative to create illusion of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance of truth, in all the incidents and conversations that occur in them, exceed any works of fiction... It is perfect illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make fiction feel real, employ minute, documentary detail (dates, log-book style), a steady narratorial persona, and the repetition of facts in varying phrases to reinforce credibility. Be aware this can lead to long relations of common incidents that may bore some readers, but it powerfully convinces 'matter-of-fact' audiences (seafaring men, poor boys, servant-maids). (Example/technique: press dates, repeat facts with phrases like 'I say...', include small procedural or quotidian specifics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the narrator distinct from the author in self-narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The _author_ never appears in these self-narratives... but the _narrator_ chains us down to an implicit belief in everything he says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing autobiographical fiction or faux-autobiography, preserve the illusion by not inserting the overt authorial presence; let the narrator's voice carry authority. Present facts and circumstantial detail as if reporting, so readers accept the account as lived experience. (Anti-pattern: overt authorial intrusions that break the illusion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt diction and style to the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: His style is everywhere beautiful, but plain and homely... written in phraseology peculiarly adapted to the lower conditions of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a register that suits your audience: 'plain and homely' diction can powerfully reach working-class or popular readers, while beauty of style need not be ornate. Consider who will read the work (e.g., seafaring men, poor boys, servant-maids) and shape phrasing and example accordingly. (Scoring note: effectiveness judged by how well style matches audience expectations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, affecting incidents grounded in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of 'Colonel Jack' is the most affecting natural picture of a young thief that was ever drawn... His losing the stolen money... and finding it again... evince a deep knowledge of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve emotional impact, include compact, psychologically convincing scenes and details that reveal character (small crises, ironies, moral perplexities). Deep observation of human behavior often trumps grand romantic plot in producing feeling and verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary presentation: neatness, handwriting, and layout matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Mary has such an invincible reluctance to any epistolary exertion... She writes such a mean, detestable hand... she is sure to omit a most substantial word in the second draught... which spoils the neatest epistle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In letters, attend to penmanship, clean first drafts (avoid excessive interlining), consistent figures and ruled lines, and decisive ink/blots. Sloppy hand, interlined corrections, errant numerals, and half-scratched smears undermine the letter's effect and can embarrass the writer. (Anti-patterns described: 'mean, detestable hand', 'lines are not less erring', 'blots... poor smears'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation choices influence creativity and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: I wrote a letter the other day in alternate lines, black ink and red, and you cannot think how it chilled the flow of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that formal or decorative experiments (e.g., alternating inks, conspicuous layout) may distract you or readers and can impede the flow of ideas. Use such devices sparingly and only when they serve expressive purpose rather than novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical career advice for authors: avoid dependence on booksellers
rubrics_metrics.description: Throw yourself on the world without any rational plan of support beyond what the chance employ of booksellers would afford you!... Keep to your bank, and the bank will keep you. Trust not to the public; you may hang, starve, drown yourself, for anything that worthy _personage_ cares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on uncertain bookseller patronage for subsistence; maintain stable, salaried employment if possible. Booksellers can be exploitative and unreliable—treat authorship as an adjunct to a secure livelihood rather than the sole means of support. (Scoring note: financial stability is a factor in sustainable literary production.)
